# Jeremiah 48:1–24 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Historical Background

Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, between the Zered and Arnon rivers. The Moabites descended from Lot's incestuous union with his elder daughter (Genesis 19:37). Historically, Moab's relations with Israel were marked by hostility—Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel (Numbers 22–24), and later Moab oppressed Israel under Eglon (Judges 3:12–14). David subdued them (2 Samuel 8:2), and they remained vassals until rebelling after Ahab's death (2 Kings 1:1; 3:4–5). By Jeremiah's time Moab had recovered territory north of the Arnon. The prophecy, according to Josephus, was fulfilled about five years after Jerusalem's fall when Nebuchadnezzar conquered Moab (c. 582 BC).

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/ ; https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-48.html

---

## Verses 1–5: Judgment Announced Against Moab's Cities

**v. 1:** *"Concerning Moab, this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: 'Woe to Nebo, for it will be devastated. Kiriathaim will be captured and disgraced; the fortress will be shattered and dismantled.'"*

- **The divine title** "LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel" asserts Yahweh's supremacy over Moab's gods and His sovereign right to judge all nations. Gill notes the phrase is also a reminder that Moab's enmity against Israel is being avenged. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- **Nebo** here is the Moabite city (Numbers 32:3, 38), not the mountain. Harrison notes it was originally built by the Reubenites. Gill suggests it may have been an oracular centre with a temple where priests gave lying oracles promising safety—making its devastation a proof of those oracles' falsity. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- **Kiriathaim** means "double city" (BDB 900). It appears as early as Genesis 14:5 and was assigned to Reuben (Joshua 13:19). Its inhabitants boasted of it as impregnable, so its capture brought them to confusion. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- **"The fortress"** (Misgab): Keil & Delitzsch argue that this is not a proper name but a designation for the highland strongholds of Moab—through Nebo's ruin and Kiriathaim's capture, the fortress in which Moab trusted is broken. Gill, however, treats Misgab as a proper name meaning "high place" or "house of their confidence." The LXX reads it as a place name. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-48.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)

**v. 2:** *"There is no longer praise for Moab; in Heshbon they devise evil against her: 'Come, let us cut her off from nationhood.' You too, O people of Madmen, will be silenced; the sword will pursue you."*

- **"No more praise of Moab"**: Kidner (cited by Enduring Word) remarks, "To us at this distance the very mention of her renown is ironic, for we can see how local and how temporary was the fame that meant so much to her." The sense is that Moab will no longer be commended as a rich, populous, fruitful country. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **Heshbon**: formerly the Amorite capital of King Sihon, later assigned to Reuben and Gad (Joshua 13:17; 21:37). By Jeremiah's time, it was the frontier town where the Babylonian army (coming from the north) plotted Moab's destruction. There is a Hebrew wordplay between *Heshbon* (חשבון) and *devised* (חשבו). Keil & Delitzsch suggest the enemy "meditate evil" here—deciding on conquest and devastation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-48.html ; https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)
- **"Cut her off from nationhood"**: Gill notes a just retaliation—Moab had once devised with others to cut off Israel (Psalm 83:4); now the same is plotted against them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- **Madmen**: The meaning is debated. There is a Hebrew wordplay between *Madmen* and *tidommi* ("be silenced / cut down"). Bible.org lists four interpretive options: (1) a wordplay on "be silenced"; (2) a wordplay on "dung hill" (cf. Isaiah 25:10); (3) a proper city name found only here; (4) a variant of Dimon/Dibon (Isaiah 15:2, 9). Peake's Commentary accepts it as a place name. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/jeremiah-48.html)

**v. 3:** *"A voice cries out from Horonaim: 'Devastation and great destruction!'"*

- **Horonaim** means "two hollows" or "two caves." It lay on a descent not far from Luhith, southward toward Zoar. The cry of "devastation and great destruction" is the content of the lament heard from that city. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- Trapp (cited by Enduring Word): "They would not cry for their sins: they shall therefore cry for their miseries with desperate and bootless tears, and yet worse one day." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)

**v. 4:** *"Moab will be shattered; her little ones will cry out."*

- **"Moab"** here probably refers to the country as a whole, not a specific city (contra some who identify it with Ar-Moab/Areopolis). Gill's Exposition notes the Targum renders it "the kingdom of Moab is broken." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-48.html)
- **"Her little ones"** (*tse'ireyha*): Some translations (RSV, NRSV) read a city name "Zoar" here (following LXX "Zogora"), but the UBS Text Project gives the MT reading "her little ones" a "B" rating—children seeing parents killed and crying out in desolation. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)

**v. 5:** *"For on the ascent to Luhith they weep bitterly as they go, and on the descent to Horonaim cries of distress resound over the destruction."*

- **Luhith**: A town on a height. The Onomasticon (cited by Keil) places it between Areopolis and Zoar. The phrase "weeping with weeping" (Hebrew doubling) means continuous, abundant weeping. Trapp says, "Hebrew, Weeping with weeping shall go up—i.e., they shall weep abundantly." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-48.html)
- The fugitives climb the ascent weeping and on the descent the enemy hears their cries of destruction. The whole geography of Moab—high and low—is filled with lamentation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)

---

## Verses 6–9: The Terror of Coming Judgment

**v. 6:** *"'Flee! Run for your lives! Become like a juniper in the desert.'"*

- The command is either the Moabites' own cry of destruction or the prophet's ironic counsel—fleeing but to no avail. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- **"Juniper"** (or "heath"): The MT reading is *ar'ar* (a destitute shrub, cf. Jeremiah 17:6). The LXX reads "wild ass," the REB "like Aroer" (a city name, matching v. 19). The UBS Text Project gives "juniper" a "C" rating (considerable doubt). The image is of being stripped, solitary, forsaken in the wilderness. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- Constable: The Moabites would be "as rare, isolated, and forsaken as juniper trees in the desert." (from search excerpt, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-48.html)

**v. 7:** *"Because you trust in your works and treasures, you too will be captured, and Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and officials."*

- **"Works"**: The Hebrew word (*ma'aseh*) can mean strongholds/fortifications (LXX, Vulgate), deeds, wealth, or idols (the works of their hands). Gill lists all these possibilities. The Septuagint favours "strongholds." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm ; https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)
- **Trust in treasures**: Moab's wealth came from trade routes and enormous flocks (2 Kings 3:4 — King Mesha paid tribute of 100,000 lambs and wool of 100,000 rams). Cundall (cited by Enduring Word) notes Moab's geographical isolation let them escape many upheavals and strengthen themselves at neighbours' expense. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **Chemosh**: The national deity of Moab (Numbers 21:29), associated with child sacrifice (2 Kings 3:27). Solomon erected a high place to Chemosh in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7), demolished under Josiah (2 Kings 23:13). The carrying off of divine statues into exile was customary for ancient Near Eastern conquerors (cf. Isaiah 46:1–2). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/ ; https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)
- Philo the Jew (cited by Gill) explains Chemosh as meaning "as groping" or "feeling"—the god of the blind, unable to see or save. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)

**v. 8:** *"The destroyer will move against every city, and not one town will escape. The valley will also be ruined, and the high plain will be destroyed, as the LORD has said."*

- **"The destroyer"**: Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonian army. The Targum reads "spoilers" in the plural. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- **"The valley"** is the Jordan Valley touching Moab on the west; **"the high plain"** (plateau/tableland) is the fertile region where most Moabite cities stood, from Aroer northward to Heshbon (Joshua 13:15–17). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-48.html)
- **"As the LORD has spoken"**: The destruction is certain because it rests on God's declared word. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)

**v. 9:** *"Put salt on Moab, for she will be laid waste; her cities will become desolate, with no one to dwell in them."*

- **"Put salt" / "Give wings"**: The Hebrew is notoriously difficult. The MT reads *tseets* ("wings")—possibly from Aramaic, used only here. The LXX reads "give signs," the NRSV "set aside salt" (from a Ugaritic root fitting judgment context, cf. Judges 9:45 where Abimelech sowed salt on a conquered city). The Vulgate reads "give a flower." Most traditional English translations read "Give wings to Moab"—either for swift escape or as a sign of swift destruction. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- Gill notes that "give wings" may signify that even with wings the Moabites could not escape—"for in flying it shall fly away," meaning swift, sudden destruction. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)

---

## Verse 10: The Cursed Sword — A Crucial Interpretive Debate

**v. 10:** *"Cursed is the one who is remiss in doing the work of the LORD, and cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed."*

This is one of the most debated verses in the chapter.

- **Traditional reading (Gill, Matthew Henry, Keil)**: This is God's charge to the Babylonians as His instruments of judgment. The "work of the LORD" is the commission to destroy Moab. They must not do it "deceitfully" (slackly, negligently) or withhold the sword. Gill compares it to Saul sparing Agag and Ahab sparing Ben-hadad—both were cursed for failing to execute full judgment. Matthew Henry applies it generally: all who have work from God—whether public ministers or private believers—must do it faithfully and with integrity. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/48.htm)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic reading (Enduring Word / David Guzik)**: Guzik emphasises that verse 10 is "not God's general endorsement of violence but a hyperbolic statement of how complete and thorough the Babylonian judgment would be—nothing held back." The Babylonians were "unknowing servants of God" and were to do their work without deceit and completely. Cundall (cited by Guzik) says this verse, described by A. S. Peake as "this bloodthirsty verse," is "not to be interpreted literally, but as a hyperbolic statement of the completeness of the judgment about to fall. Such an event inevitably involves bloodshed, but the Lord takes no delight in the death of the most rebellious sinner (cf. 2 Peter 3:9)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)

- **Evangelical reading (Bible.org)**: Many English translations (TEV, NJB, NET) mark this verse as a parenthesis addressed to the Babylonian invaders, admonishing them to fully execute YHWH's judgment—"Show no mercy!" (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)

- **Peake's Commentary (modern critical)**: Peake regarded this as "a bloodthirsty verse" and considered it possibly an interpolation—a later addition. (Referenced by Cundall in Enduring Word.)

- **Kidner** (cited in Enduring Word) notes "the fearful twist to what may well have been a proverb or preacher's text in verse 10a (*Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord with slackness*), turning it into a charge to Moab's executioners." This suggests the first half of the verse had a known proverbial use for spiritual diligence, here grimly redirected. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)

---

## Verses 11–13: The Wine Metaphor — Moab's Complacency

**v. 11:** *"Moab has been at ease from youth, settled like wine on its dregs; he has not been poured from vessel to vessel or gone into exile. So his flavor has remained the same, and his aroma is unchanged."*

- **The wine-making image**: In ancient wine-making, after fermentation, wine sat in jars and the dregs (impurities) settled at the bottom. It was then carefully poured into another vessel, leaving the dregs behind. Repeating this process several times produced refined wine with fewer impurities. Moab, however, had never been "emptied from vessel to vessel"—never unsettled by invasion, exile, or upheaval. The dregs therefore remained and spoiled the wine. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **Spiritual meaning (Gill)**: Moab is an emblem of unregenerate sinners—"at ease from youth," settled on the lees of corruption, never emptied of sin or self-righteousness, their "taste" for sin and "scent" of worldliness unchanged. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- **Morgan**: "One secret of the corruption of Moab had been that of its comparative ease." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **Kidner**: "For defence, Moab had towering cliffs, and for wealth, her enormous flocks of sheep, riches that were self-renewing. But the shelter of these things had bred more complacency than character." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **Thompson**: "She lay outside the normal route of the invaders of the Middle East and was rarely disturbed." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **Matthew Henry**: Security and trusting in wealth and strength are among the sins for which God now reckons with Moab. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/48.htm)

**v. 12:** *"Therefore behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will send to him wanderers, who will pour him out. They will empty his vessels and shatter his jars."*

- **"Wanderers"** (or "travellers" / "wine-workers"): The Hebrew *tso'im* can mean those who cause wine to travel from vessel to vessel—"wine coopers" or "tippers." Gill notes the Chaldeans are meant: they wandered from their own country to Moab and would cause the Moabites to wander into exile. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- Continuing the wine metaphor, God now sends "wine-workers" (Babylon) to tip Moab over roughly, empty the vessels, and smash the jars—a violent racking, not the gentle decanting of fine wine. Feinberg says: "Unlike an earthenware jar that is carefully tilted so as not to lose the sediment of the wine, Moab will be roughly dealt with ('pour her out') and emptied like jars and smashed like jugs." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **Application (Enduring Word)**: For the believer under the new covenant, being "emptied from vessel to vessel" is a work of God's goodness and compassion—refining rather than destroying. But for Moab it was pure judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)

**v. 13:** *"Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, just as the house of Israel was ashamed when they trusted in Bethel."*

- **Chemosh**: Moab's god would prove powerless. The people would be ashamed of having trusted him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **Bethel**: This refers to the northern kingdom of Israel's idolatrous calf-worship established by Jeroboam I (1 Kings 12:25–33). When the Assyrians conquered Israel (722 BC), the northern tribes learned the impotence of their false worship centre at Bethel. Moab would learn the same lesson about Chemosh. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- Gill notes the irony: Israel's shame over Bethel should have been a warning to Moab, but Moab persisted in its own idolatry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)

---

## Verses 14–17: The Calamity Draws Near

**v. 14:** *"How can you say, 'We are warriors, mighty men ready for battle'?"*

- Moab boasted of military strength. This was a false confidence that God directly challenges. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- Harrison notes that Moab had never undergone the experience of exile, though invaded periodically—this bred overconfidence. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)

**v. 15:** *"Moab has been destroyed and its towns have been invaded; the best of its young men have gone down in the slaughter, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts."*

- **"The King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts"**: This is a majestic title, contrasting Yahweh as the true King over all nations against Chemosh, the false god. It is not a local deity who speaks, but the King who commands the armies of heaven. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- The "best" (*mivchar*) young men—the choice warriors—go down to slaughter. Moab's pride in its warriors is humiliated. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)

**v. 16:** *"Moab's calamity is at hand, and his affliction is rushing swiftly."*

- The destruction is both certain and imminent. Keil & Delitzsch place this in the strophe describing how "Moab's glory is departed." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-48.html)

**v. 17:** *"Mourn for him, all you who surround him, everyone who knows his name; tell how the mighty scepter is shattered—the glorious staff!"*

- **"Mighty scepter" and "glorious staff"**: Royal symbols of power and dominion. Thompson notes they "refer back to the days when Moab was able to exert some influence in the neighboring areas (Jeremiah 27:3; 2 Kings 1:1; 3:4–5; 24:2)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- Bible.org notes these are both royal symbols: (1) *scepter* (matteh)—a staff/rod of rule; (2) *staff* (maqqel)—could refer to a shepherd's staff, a traveller's stick, a weapon, or a diviner's rod. Here it refers to the kingdom of Moab. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)
- Surrounding nations are called to lament—even Moab's neighbours should recognise the tragedy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)

---

## Verses 18–24: The Complete Conquest

**v. 18:** *"Come down from your glory; sit on parched ground, O daughter dwelling in Dibon, for the destroyer of Moab has come against you; he has destroyed your fortresses."*

- **Dibon** (modern Dhiban) was four miles north of the Arnon and thirteen miles east of the Dead Sea. It was the location where the famous **Moabite Stone** (Mesha Stele) was discovered in 1868. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **"Come down from your glory; sit on parched ground"**: A call to descend from the elevated, proud city and sit in thirst/dust—a posture of humiliation. The Anchor Bible (cited by Bible.org) lists possible readings: "filth/excrement," "thirst" (MT), or "on parched ground" (cf. Isaiah 44:3). (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)
- Keil & Delitzsch note the feminine singular address personifies Dibon as a "daughter" brought low. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-48.html)

**v. 19:** *"Stand by the road and watch, O dweller of Aroer! Ask the man fleeing or the woman escaping, 'What has happened?'"*

- **Aroer** stood on the northern edge of the Arnon gorge, situated to observe fugitives crossing the river. The inhabitants are to watch the road and ask the refugees what has occurred. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-48.html)
- The scene is vivid—both men and women are fleeing, indicating total collapse.

**v. 20:** *"Moab is put to shame, for it has been shattered. Wail and cry out! Declare by the Arnon that Moab is destroyed."*

- **"By the Arnon"**: The Arnon River (Wadi Mujib) was the major boundary of Moab. The news of Moab's destruction is to be proclaimed at this defining landmark. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- Bible.org notes textual variants (Kethiv/Qere issues) in the imperatives "wail" and "cry out" regarding feminine singular vs. masculine plural forms—reflecting the difficulty of whether the nation is addressed as feminine or the inhabitants as masculine. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)

**vv. 21–24:** *"Judgment has come upon the high plain—upon Holon, Jahzah, and Mephaath, upon Dibon, Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim, upon Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon, upon Kerioth, Bozrah, and all the towns of Moab, those far and near."*

- The list of cities conveys the **completeness** of judgment. Enduring Word notes at least 14 specific places are enumerated to give a sense that no corner of Moab escapes. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- Bible.org provides identifications where known: Holon (possibly the same as Horon), Jahzah (cf. Isaiah 15:4), Mephaath (Joshua 13:18; 21:37), Kerioth (cf. Amos 2:2), Bozrah (not the Edomite Bozrah of Jeremiah 49:13). Several sites remain unidentified. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)
- **"The high plain"** (*erets hammishor*): the plateau or tableland where most Moabite cities were situated. Constable notes this is the fertile tableland from Aroer northward to Heshbon (Joshua 13:15–17). (from search excerpt, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-48.html)
- Constable: "Jeremiah listed 11 other cities of Moab that would experience destruction—representing all the towns in the nation." (from search excerpt)
- Peake's Commentary notes that several of these sites are unknown; Bozrah here is not the Edomite city. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/jeremiah-48.html)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The main hermeneutical differences among traditions on this passage concern **verse 10** and the nature of God's judgment:

### Verse 10 — The "Cursed Sword"

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word): Emphasises the hyperbolic nature; God takes no delight in bloodshed. This is about thoroughness of judgment, not a universal endorsement of violence. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **Reformed Baptist (Gill)** and **Puritan (Matthew Henry)**: Read it as a general principle of faithful service to God, applied specifically to the Chaldeans as instruments. The curse is on doing God's work "deceitfully" (slackly, half-heartedly). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/48.htm)
- **Evangelical (Bible.org)**: Treats it as a parenthesis addressed to Babylon, emphasising thorough execution of divine judgment. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)
- **Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch)**: Reads it straightforwardly as God's charge to the destroyers, part of the calamities-strophe without extensive qualification. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-48.html)
- **Modern critical (Peake)**: Regards it as "bloodthirsty" and possibly a later interpolation—not authentic to Jeremiah. (Referenced in Enduring Word.)

### The Wine Metaphor (vv. 11–12)

- **Gill (Baptist)** explicitly allegorises it as a picture of the unregenerate sinner—settled in corruption, never emptied of sin or self-righteousness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal)** distinguishes between Old Covenant judgment (God pours out wrath on Moab) and New Covenant application (God refines believers through hardship out of love). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
- **Morgan (Evangelical/Exposition)** emphasises the cause: Moab's "comparative ease" as the secret of its corruption. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)

### Pride as the Root Sin

All traditions agree that pride is the foundational sin of Moab (v. 29, cf. v. 42), but emphases differ:

- **Matthew Henry (Puritan)** amplifies this at length: pride is "mentioned six times," described with "multiplying of words to the same purport," showing how "offensive it was both to God and man." Moab scorned Israel in their troubles and magnified themselves against the LORD. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/48.htm)
- **Parker (The People's Bible)** emphasises the moral basis of judgment: "The destruction, therefore, was not arbitrary, but moral, being based upon an assigned reason. 'Pride goeth before destruction.'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jpb/jeremiah-48.html)

---

## Other Views (Modern Scholarship)

### Text-Critical and Source Issues

- **Peake's Commentary** notes that "much of this chapter is almost certainly later than Jeremiah, as it incorporates parts of Isaiah 15f., an elegy apparently of the fifth century." Jeremiah 48 draws heavily on Isaiah 15–16, adapting older oracles for a new context. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/jeremiah-48.html)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** acknowledge the dependence on Isaiah but defend Jeremiah's originality: "Jeremiah accordingly takes up anew the utterances of the old prophets regarding Moab which had not yet been fulfilled, but were now about to receive their accomplishment: these he reproduces in his own peculiar manner." They reject the charge of "feeble imitation" levelled by Gesenius and others. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-48.html)
- **Bible.org** provides a chart showing the close literary relationship between Isaiah 15–16 and Jeremiah 48, with at least 14 parallel passages. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)

### Translation Difficulties

- **v. 6 "juniper"**: The LXX reads "wild ass"; some modern translations read "like Aroer" (a city). The MT is uncertain. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)
- **v. 9 "put salt" / "give wings"**: The NRSV adopts a Ugaritic root meaning "salt" (for judgment); traditional English Bibles read "wings." Consensus is lacking. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)
- **v. 18 "parched ground"**: The Anchor Bible lists options including "filth/excrement," "thirst," and "on parched ground." The JPSOA footnote says "Meaning of the Heb. uncertain." (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)

---

## Summary of Key Themes (vv. 1–24)

1. **God's universal sovereignty**: Yahweh is not merely Israel's God but "LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel" who judges all nations. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
2. **The danger of complacency**: Moab's long ease, geographical isolation, and prosperity bred pride, self-reliance, and spiritual decay. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/48.htm)
3. **False trusts exposed**: Moab trusted in fortifications, treasures, warriors, and Chemosh—all of which would fail. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/48.htm)
4. **Judgment is certain and complete**: No city escapes; the list of place names drives home totality. (https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-48)
5. **Judgment is moral, not arbitrary**: Rooted in pride, idolatry, and mistreatment of God's people. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jpb/jeremiah-48.html)
6. **God's strange work**: Even deserved judgment is grieved by God and the prophet, pointing toward the ultimate hope of restoration (v. 47). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/)
